cleared.check: Critic lead from cycle 1, second half: does any function an ordinary account can call change balanceOf(PoolManager) on Arbitrum One without a transfer, so that a settle is credited for it.
cleared.result: Of 29 token addresses tried, the ones whose balance moves without transfers are four Aave aTokens. Their balance depends on the block timestamp and on the reserve index, and the Aave pool reports that the whole flash loan premium goes to the protocol, so no call inside one transaction raises the index. A sync and a settle in the same transaction therefore see the same balance. The time based growth is recorded as a low finding. The sample is not the full token list of the PoolManager, which I could not obtain.

cleared.check: Can one owner change or withdraw another owner's position through modifyLiquidity, including by reusing a salt, by passing ticks of another position, or by removing more than it holds.
cleared.result: No. The position is looked up under keccak256 of owner, tickLower, tickUpper and salt, and the owner is always msg.sender (src/PoolManager.sol:161, src/libraries/Position.sol:34-41). The assembly lays the four fields out as 20, 3, 3 and 32 bytes without overlap, and bytes above the address fall outside the hashed range (Position.sol:54-66). I rebuilt the layout byte for byte and compared it with the packed encoding that test/libraries/Position.t.sol:75-80 expects on 3,000 random inputs, with dirty upper bits in the owner word. A removal larger than the position reverts in LiquidityMath.addDelta (Position.sol:88, src/libraries/LiquidityMath.sol:10-18), after the tick updates, and the revert undoes those. In 6,000 random sequences on a Python transcription, every attempt by a second owner, by the same owner under a different salt, or for one unit more than the position held reverted.

cleared.check: Order of the steps inside Pool.modifyLiquidity: tick update, bitmap flip, fee growth read, Position.update, tick clearing, and the three price cases for the amounts. Covered add, remove, zero delta, full range, one spacing, ranges above, below and around the current tick, and several owners on shared ticks.
cleared.result: The order is sound. A new tick gets its feeGrowthOutside before the fee growth inside the range is read (src/libraries/Pool.sol:160-162, 533-539, 184-185). A tick whose liquidityGross returns to zero is deleted only after the last position has been paid from its values (Pool.sol:187-203). A position that still has liquidity keeps both its ticks alive, because liquidityGross is the sum of the positions on the tick, so its checkpoint can never meet a re-initialized tick. A position with zero liquidity earns nothing at its next update because fees use the liquidity held before the update (src/libraries/Position.sol:82-97). Amounts use slot0.tick for the range test and the stored sqrt price for the in range case, add rounds up and remove rounds down (Pool.sol:206-237, src/libraries/SqrtPriceMath.sol:261-288). I transcribed Pool, Position, TickBitmap, LiquidityMath, SqrtPriceMath, SwapMath and TickMath into Python and ran 6,000 random sequences (254,069 operations, 50,789 of them reverts) with four owners, two salts, spacings 1, 10, 60, 200, 2000 and 32767, start prices in the middle and within 3,000 ticks of both ends, swaps, donations and protocol fees. After every operation liquidityGross and liquidityNet of each tick equalled the sums over positions, the bitmap bit was set exactly for ticks with liquidityGross above zero, pool liquidity equalled the liquidity of positions in range at slot0.tick, and the pool never owed more of either currency than it had received. At the end every position could be removed in full and all tick data was gone. A second set of 6,000 sequences without swaps or donations, 3,614 of them started in the state where slot0.tick is one below the tick of the price, paid no fees to anyone and left no owner with more than it had paid in.

cleared.check: Can an ordinary account make a hookless victim position impossible to remove, or leave a tick that can no longer be updated. Listed every revert on the removal path.
cleared.result: No path found for a token with fewer than 2^127 base units. On removal the cap is not checked (src/libraries/Pool.sol:165). liquidityGross cannot underflow because it is the sum of the positions. liquidityNet stays inside int128 because its size is bounded by liquidityGross, and the cap is at most 6076470837873901133274546561281575204 (spacing 32767), below 2^127. The same bound keeps pool liquidity inside uint128 when ticks are crossed. flipTick cannot revert for a tick that was initialized, since only aligned ticks can be initialized (src/libraries/TickBitmap.sol:47-75). FullMath.mulDiv in Position.update cannot revert because the product of a 256 bit growth difference and a 128 bit liquidity divided by 2^128 fits in 256 bits. The casts of the principal amounts can revert for a very large position, and the owner then removes in parts. The sum of principal and fees can exceed int128, and the owner then collects fees with a zero delta first (src/PoolManager.sol:171). What remains is the known case of uncollected fees of 2^127 base units or more (F-005). I checked whether flash accounting gives a cheaper route to that bound: it does not. An account that is the only liquidity in range can donate to itself at no cost and wrap feeGrowthGlobal past 2^256, as the comment at Pool.sol:80-82 says, but positions out of range see no change in their fee growth inside, and after later tick crossings they are owed only real swap fees (six self donations of 2^127 - 1 units in the transcription, then swaps through both victim ranges). When a victim is in range, its share of a donation is real value the donor has to pay.

cleared.check: Hook deltas on liquidity changes: can afterAddLiquidity or afterRemoveLiquidity move more than the caller's own delta, which hook runs for a zero delta, and what a hook that calls modifyLiquidity itself can skip.
cleared.result: The caller delta after the hook is the pool delta minus the hook delta, and the hook is credited the hook delta, so the two always add up to principal plus fees (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:219-244, src/PoolManager.sol:171-183). The hook delta is read only when the matching return-delta bit is set, and then the return data must be exactly 64 bytes (Hooks.sol:159-168). A zero delta runs the remove hooks (Hooks.sol:201-205, 220-244). When the hook itself is the caller, the hook calls are skipped and no delta is taken (Hooks.sol:171-175, 217). A pool without a hook has none of these paths. The hazard for pools whose liquidity providers chose a hook is already recorded as F-004. One comment differs from the code: src/interfaces/IHooks.sol:50 and 81 say the delta passed to the after hooks includes the hook delta, while the code passes principal plus fees before the hook delta is known. This changes no balance.

cleared.check: donate from entry to the last delta: who is debited, who can receive, rounding, the tick and price mismatch at a boundary, and whether a donation can be redirected away from positions that were in range.
cleared.result: The donor is debited the two amounts, each cast to int128, and fee growth rises by amount times 2^128 divided by the liquidity in range, rounded down (src/libraries/Pool.sol:466-480, src/PoolManager.sol:256-276). A donation reverts when no liquidity is in range. The rounding remainder is below one base unit per donation and stays in the PoolManager. In the transcription each in range position was owed at most its exact share and the shares never added up to more than the donation, across all donations in 6,000 sequences. Positions out of range were unchanged. The two concrete values of test/PoolManager.t.sol:841-864 (34028236692093846346337 and 68056473384187692692674 for 100 and 200 units on 1e18 liquidity) come out of the source formula. Two things can redirect a donation, and both are stated in src/interfaces/IPoolManager.sol:150-155: liquidity added just before the donation takes a share, and after a zeroForOne swap that ends exactly on a tick, slot0.tick is one below the tick of the price, so the donation goes to the range below. Both cost the donor's intended recipients future income and take nothing that a position already holds.

cleared.check: Do the liquidity related tests in the repository hold against the source text: test/libraries/TickBitmap.t.sol, LiquidityMath.t.sol, Position.t.sol, SafeCast.t.sol, the modifyLiquidity fuzz in test/libraries/Pool.t.sol:43-84, the salt tests and the two fixed cases of test/ModifyLiquidity.t.sol, and the liquidity and donate cases of test/PoolManager.t.sol.
cleared.result: All hold. The 18 fixed vectors of TickBitmap.t.sol for nextInitializedTickWithinOneWord, the flip sequences, and the fuzz properties for compress, flipTick alignment, the search on the fixture bitmap and the search on an empty bitmap passed on the transcription (20,000 random inputs each). LiquidityMath: the three revert cases, addDelta(2^127, -2^127) = 0 and the int128 minimum fuzz passed. Position: the position hash and the revert conditions of the update fuzz passed. SafeCast: the conditions in the source are the ones the tests state. Pool.t.sol: the order of expected reverts (ticks misordered, lower bound, upper bound, underflow for a negative delta, empty position for zero, cap on the lower tick, misaligned lower, misaligned upper, int128 overflow of an amount) is the order in which the source reaches them. ModifyLiquidity.t.sol: the salt and router separation tests follow from the position hash, and the two fixed cases (spacing 32767 and spacing 1) are within one pip of the closed form, with differences of one base unit from rounding up. PoolManager.t.sol: ManagerLocked comes before PoolNotInitialized, and the donate reverts and values match. The JavaScript reference of the ffi fuzz test was not run.

cleared.check: Does the liquidity path give the same amounts on each network's EVM. Sent read-only eth_call probes to the PositionManager listed in networks.json: a multicall that initializes a new native pool and mints a position above the price, and a second set that mints and burns the same position in one call. Each probe was sent once with exactly the value the source formulas require and once with one wei less.
cleared.result: All 20 networks agree with the source formulas to the wei. Mint probes (9 per network): the highest tick filled to the cap for spacings 1, 60 and 200 (519766372, 1878783905959 and 20966766746469 wei, and TickLiquidityOverflow for one unit above the cap), a range next to a mid price, a range from tick -887190 to 887270 whose amount is 9185290247808691312573729382907766498, a range next to the lowest tick, spacing 32767, the largest liquidity whose amount stays below 2^127 (amount 170141183460469231731687013724867035278 accepted) and the next step above it (SafeCastOverflow). Mint and burn probes (6 per network): the caller owes exactly one wei, which is the gap between rounding up on add and rounding down on remove, and the call fails with zero value. These probes exercise TickMath, the 512 bit multiply and divide, signed tick arithmetic, the bitmap, the position hash, tick clearing, transient deltas and native settlement. Two side observations. The Soneium PositionManager holds 176652317140 wei that any caller's payment can draw on, so on Soneium the probe values were reduced by that balance, and the one wei less variant could not be tested for the spacing 1 mint and for the six mint and burn probes. On BNB Smart Chain the token id has to be read at a pinned block because new positions are minted every block. The probes ran against public RPC nodes at the latest block on 2026-11-22 and say nothing about validator builds. Donations and fee collection were not probed on chain because no deployed periphery contract exposes donate.

cleared.check: Same question for Tempo, where the node answers any call that carries value with 'value transfer not allowed' and eth_getBalance returns the constant 4242424242424242424242424242424242424242424242424242424242424242424242424242 for the PositionManager.
cleared.result: Partly covered. The value probes cannot run on Tempo. I used a probe that needs no payment: a position on ticks -887271 to -887270 of a new pool at the lowest price, with liquidity equal to a multiple of the product of the two sqrt prices, so that the amount on add and on remove is exact and the caller owes nothing. Mint and burn in one call succeeded on Tempo and on Ethereum for multiples 1 and 7, failed on both for liquidity one unit higher or lower (one base unit owed), and reverted on both with SafeCastOverflow for multiple 1000003, whose amount is above 2^127. An add that is paid in a TIP-20 currency was not probed. A pool with currency address(0) can be initialized on Tempo but can never receive a payment, so it holds nothing.

cleared.check: Lead L-133, second half: is there a hook that must add liquidity on a tick an attacker can fill cheaply. Read the Zora coin hook, which adds liquidity inside afterSwap.
cleared.result: Not affected at realistic prices. CoinRewardsV4.mintLpReward runs inside afterSwap without a try block and adds a position one spacing wide that starts two spacings away from the current tick (CoinRewardsV4.sol lines 134-204, ZoraV4CoinHook.sol line 415 on the main branch). A full tick there would make every swap in the pool revert. The fill cost near the current tick is the cap times about 0.01 divided by the sqrt price in currency0, or times the sqrt price in currency1. With the cap of 3.8e34 for spacing 200 this is above the whole supply of a coin with 1e27 base units unless the price ratio in base units is beyond about 1e11, which only the far ends of the tick range reach. I read the repository source and did not check that the deployed hooks run this code.

cleared.check: Line by line trace of a swap in a pool without a hook, from PoolManager.swap to the last delta written, for exact input and exact output in both directions.
cleared.result: swap rejects a zero amount and an uninitialized pool before anything else (src/PoolManager.sol:193-196). With hooks equal to address(0) beforeSwap returns the caller's amount unchanged and afterSwap returns a zero hook delta, because no permission bit is set (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:252-255, 298, 306). Pool.swap treats a negative amount as exact input and a positive amount as exact output at every place that branches on it (src/libraries/Pool.sol:313, 371, 453; src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:61). For exact input the remaining amount rises toward zero by amountIn plus fee and the calculated amount grows by amountOut. For exact output the remaining amount falls by amountOut and the calculated amount falls by amountIn plus fee (Pool.sol:371-382). The final delta puts the specified amount in currency1 exactly when zeroForOne differs from exact input (Pool.sol:453-461), so the caller is debited the input currency and credited the output currency in all four cases. Both casts to int128 revert on overflow (Pool.sol:455, 459; src/libraries/SafeCast.sol:40-43). The protocol fee is booked to the input currency (PoolManager.sol:216, 238). _accountPoolBalanceDelta writes amount0 to currency0 and amount1 to currency1 for msg.sender (PoolManager.sol:226, 381-384). I found no step where a sign, an operand order or a cast gives the caller more than the pool math computed.

cleared.check: beforeSwap: the returned delta, the check that the swap type does not change, and the fee override word, including a hook that returns dirty upper bits.
cleared.result: The hook result must be exactly 96 bytes and start with the beforeSwap selector, otherwise the call reverts (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:152-154, 259). The specified delta is read only when the address carries BEFORE_SWAP_RETURNS_DELTA_FLAG (Hooks.sol:266-270). It is added to the caller's amount with checked arithmetic, and the call reverts when an exact input amount becomes positive or an exact output amount becomes negative (Hooks.sol:273-278). An amount of exactly zero is allowed and makes Pool.swap return a zero delta without touching state (src/libraries/Pool.sol:320). The fee word is read only for a dynamic fee pool (Hooks.sol:263). parseFee assigns a full 32 byte word to a uint24 in assembly (src/libraries/ParseBytes.sol:16-21). The value is then used only through isOverride, which ANDs with 0x400000, and removeOverrideFlag, which ANDs with 0xBFFFFF, followed by a comparison with 1,000,000 (src/libraries/LPFeeLibrary.sol:61-78, Pool.sol:303-305). Both masks are 24 bit constants, so upper bits supplied by the hook cannot reach the fee, whatever the compiler does with the assignment. Without the override bit the stored fee is used. A hook can set the fee of its own dynamic fee pool to any value from 0 to 100 percent, which is the recorded hook trust finding F-004 and does not reach pools without that hook.

cleared.check: afterSwap and the two _accountDelta calls: does the caller delta plus the hook delta always equal the pool delta, and can a cast or a packing step lose a value.
cleared.result: afterSwap takes the specified and unspecified parts of the beforeSwap return, adds the afterSwap return to the unspecified part with a checked int128 cast and a checked addition (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:295-303), places the two parts in currency order with the same rule that Pool.swap uses (Hooks.sol:307-309 against src/libraries/Pool.sol:453), and subtracts the hook delta from the swap delta (Hooks.sol:312). The subtraction works on sign extended halves and reverts when a half leaves the int128 range (src/types/BalanceDelta.sol:34-46). PoolManager.swap then credits the hook delta to the hook address and the remainder to msg.sender (src/PoolManager.sol:221-226). The pool was run with the adjusted amount, so the two accounts together receive exactly the pool delta and each must reach zero before unlock returns (PoolManager.sol:112). I transcribed these lines and ran 20,000 random combinations of direction, amount and hook delta. Caller plus hook equalled the pool delta in every accepted case, and the accepted and rejected cases matched the conditions written in test/CustomAccounting.t.sol:195-209.

cleared.check: Fee split between protocol and liquidity providers in each step, and the unchecked subtraction of the protocol share.
cleared.result: The swap fee is the LP fee when the protocol fee is zero and protocolFee + lpFee - floor(protocolFee * lpFee / 1e6) otherwise (src/libraries/Pool.sol:307, src/libraries/ProtocolFeeLibrary.sol:38-46). It equals the protocol fee only when the LP fee is zero, because the protocol fee field is 12 bits wide and capped at 1,000. In that case the whole step fee goes to the protocol. Otherwise the protocol receives floor((amountIn + feeAmount) * protocolFee / 1e6) and the rest goes to fee growth (Pool.sol:391-405). In 300,000 random step shapes over the whole price range, with liquidity from 0 to 2^127 and amounts up to 2^255, the protocol share never exceeded the step fee, so the unchecked subtraction at Pool.sol:395 did not wrap. The transcribed swap reproduced the protocol fee totals that test/PoolManager.t.sol:779-818 and test/DynamicFees.t.sol:286-318 expect in 12,000 random cases, including the rounding up when the LP fee is zero. Rounding favours liquidity providers over the protocol and never the swapper.

cleared.check: Rounding of every amount in a swap step, asking who gains if a result is off by one unit.
cleared.result: Exact input: the amount after fee is rounded down, the input needed to reach the target is rounded up, the fee on a full step is rounded up, the fee on a partial step is the whole remainder, and the output is rounded down (src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:64-86). Exact output: the output to the target is rounded down, the input and the fee are rounded up (SwapMath.sol:88-104). The next price is rounded up when currency0 comes in and down when currency1 comes in, which moves the price less than the exact result for an input and more for an output (src/libraries/SqrtPriceMath.sol:31-120, 146-148, 175-177). Every rounding step is against the swapper. The transcription returned the values asserted in test/libraries/SwapMath.t.sol:69-180 for seven fixed vectors and the Swap event values asserted in test/DynamicFees.t.sol:156-279, test/DynamicReturnFees.t.sol:94, test/PoolManager.t.sol:501-503 and 608.

cleared.check: Tick crossing, the sign of liquidityNet, the tick stored after a step, and the price limit bounds.
cleared.result: The loop asks the bitmap for the next tick at or below the current tick when zeroForOne and above it otherwise (src/libraries/Pool.sol:347-348, src/libraries/TickBitmap.sol:94-119), clamps the result to MIN_TICK and MAX_TICK (Pool.sol:351-356) and uses the nearer of that tick's price and the limit as the target (src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:25-36). A crossing happens only when the step ends exactly on the price of an initialized tick. It flips both fee growth outside values with the updated growth of the input currency and applies liquidityNet with its sign reversed for zeroForOne (Pool.sol:413-428, 602-612). After a zeroForOne step that ends on a tick the stored tick is one below it (Pool.sol:431). I traced the following oneForZero swap, a liquidity add on each side of that tick and a donate from that state. Each of them treats the pool as sitting just below the tick, which agrees with the liquidity value the swap left. A zeroForOne limit must be above MIN_SQRT_PRICE and a oneForZero limit below MAX_SQRT_PRICE (Pool.sol:322-338), so a swap cannot cross MIN_TICK downward or reach the price of MAX_TICK. Addition of liquidityNet reverts above 2^128 - 1 (src/libraries/LiquidityMath.sol:10-19) and the per tick cap keeps the sum over all ticks below that bound (Pool.sol:165-173, 565-582). The transcription returned the next tick and the initialized flag asserted in 19 fixed cases of test/libraries/TickBitmap.t.sol:130-293 and met its two fuzz properties in 40,000 random cases.

cleared.check: Extremes of tick, price, liquidity, amount and fee, tested as solvency of one pool: can any sequence make a pool pay out more of a currency than it took in. This matters for every pool, because the PoolManager keeps no reserve per pool and a pool that overpays would draw on the balances of the others.
cleared.result: I wrote a third transcription of FullMath, UnsafeMath, BitMath, TickMath, SqrtPriceMath, SwapMath, LiquidityMath, TickBitmap, the position update and Pool.initialize, modifyLiquidity, swap and donate from the source text, with 256 bit wrapping where the source is unchecked or assembly. I checked it against the fixed values in the repository tests named in the other items. I then ran 8,000 random sequences of 5 to 40 operations: tick spacings 1, 10, 60, 200, 32767 and random, starting prices over the whole range including MIN_TICK and the ticks next to MAX_TICK, static fees from 0 to 100 percent, a per swap fee override in 40 percent of the swaps, protocol fees from 0 to 1,000 in both directions, liquidity up to 2^126, exact input and exact output amounts up to 2^255 with both the extreme and nearby price limits, and donations up to 2^126. After every operation, and after all positions were removed, the net amount the pool had received in each currency was at least the protocol fee accrued, in all 8,000 runs. 17 runs ended with a position that could not be removed. In each of them the fees paid into the pool in one currency exceeded 2^127 base units, which is the recorded finding F-005 and cannot happen for a token whose supply is below 2^127.

cleared.check: Zero liquidity in range: a swap step with liquidity 0 moves the price for free. Can that give the swapper tokens or damage positions.
cleared.result: With liquidity 0 the input to the target, the output and the fee are all 0, the step reaches its target and no fee growth is added (src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:66-74, 84-90; src/libraries/Pool.sol:401). In the transcription a swap of 1e18 exact input through an empty range returned the delta (0, 0) and only moved the price and tick. Positions are not affected, because a later add or removal computes its amounts from the price and tick of that moment with the usual rounding (Pool.sol:206-237) and the solvency runs above include such moves. The free move matters for contracts that read a pool price as an oracle and for the gas cost recorded in the finding of this unit. It does not move funds in core.

cleared.check: Swap hook calls to an address that is a precompile, a system contract or an account without code: can the PoolManager be made to accept such a call during a swap.
cleared.result: callHook reverts unless the call succeeds and the return data is at least 32 bytes that start with the selector that was sent (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-155). An address without code returns nothing and fails this test. beforeSwap also needs exactly 96 bytes (Hooks.sol:259) and afterSwap with the return delta flag exactly 64 bytes (Hooks.sol:166). A contract that returns its input unchanged passes the selector test but returns the whole call data, which is longer than 96 bytes for beforeSwap and longer than 64 bytes for afterSwap, so it cannot act as a swap hook that returns deltas. It can only pass as an afterSwap hook without the return delta flag, where the return value is ignored (Hooks.sol:163). A failed hook call reverts the whole swap, so a side effect in the callee does not survive. Such a pool is one that somebody chose to create with that address as hook, and pools without a hook never make these calls.

cleared.check: A native asset that also answers as an ERC-20 at some address: can sync, settle and take, in any order, credit one payment twice or credit more than was paid. Exhaustive search over a model of src/PoolManager.sol:279-297 and 349-364.
cleared.result: I modelled the PoolManager balance, the synced currency, the synced reserves, the two deltas and the attacker's wallet, with operations sync(0), sync(face), settle with value, settle without value, take in each currency, a transfer through the face and a native transfer that reaches the PoolManager without a call. I searched every sequence of up to 6 operations with amounts 1, 2 and 3. When the face reports the native balance one to one, no sequence left the attacker better off. The guard at PoolManager.sol:356 blocks the only order that would count a value twice. When the face reports floor(native / S) for S above 1, the best sequence gained S - 1 base units per round of sync and settle, and it needs native value to arrive without a call while the face is synced. On Arc the USDC contract at 0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000 returns decimals 6 and its balanceOf for the PoolManager equalled floor(eth_getBalance / 1e12) at blocks 0x1f14a00, 0x1f14a63 and 0x1f14a79, with remainders of 930109466545, 178438878313 and 971982015932 base units. S is therefore 1e12 there and one round can gain less than 0.000001 USDC. I did not test whether native USDC can reach the PoolManager without a call on Arc, and I did not query the one to one property on Celo and Polygon again. For those two I rely on the earlier findings F-023 and F-008.
cleared.source: src/PoolManager.sol:279-297, 349-364; https://rpc.mainnet.arc.io eth_call decimals() and balanceOf(PoolManager) on 0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000 and eth_getBalance at blocks 0x1f14a00, 0x1f14a63, 0x1f14a79

cleared.check: Slot0 packing: field offsets, mask widths, sign handling of the tick and the effect of dirty upper bits passed to a setter.
cleared.result: The four fields sit at bit offsets 0, 160, 184 and 208 with widths 160, 24, 24 and 24, so they end at bit 232 and do not overlap (src/types/Slot0.sol:33-38). MASK_160_BITS is written with 42 hex digits, two of them leading zeros, and equals 2^160 - 1. Every setter ANDs the new value with its mask before the shift and clears only its own field in the packed word (Slot0.sol:66-93). The tick getter sign extends from 24 bits (Slot0.sol:47-51). I transcribed the eight functions into Python and ran 200,000 random cases in which each setter received a full 256 bit value. Every getter returned the input truncated to the field width, the top 24 bits of the word stayed unchanged, and the order of the setters did not change the result. No caller-supplied value can spill into a neighbouring field. The repository test test/types/Slot0.t.sol:8-35 states the same round trip and the source text satisfies it.

cleared.check: BalanceDelta and BeforeSwapDelta packing and unpacking, and the arithmetic on packed deltas.
cleared.result: toBalanceDelta shifts amount0 left by 128 bits and masks amount1 to 128 bits, so sign extension bits of a negative amount1 cannot reach amount0 (src/types/BalanceDelta.sol:14-18). amount0 is read with sar 128 and amount1 with signextend 15 (BalanceDelta.sol:61-71). add and sub split both operands, add or subtract the halves as 256 bit numbers and pass each half through SafeCast.toInt128, which reverts when the result leaves the int128 range (BalanceDelta.sol:20-46, src/libraries/SafeCast.sol:40-43). A carry from the low half therefore cannot enter the high half. BeforeSwapDelta uses the same layout with the specified amount in the high half (src/types/BeforeSwapDelta.sol:9-37). A Python transcription returned the inputs for 200,000 random int128 pairs and for the extreme pairs. The hook delta that reaches these functions is a full word chosen by the hook, and both halves are valid int128 values by construction, so no bit pattern is out of range.

cleared.check: Fee fields: LP fee bounds and flag bits, the two 12 bit protocol fee halves, the combined swap fee and the unchecked subtraction of the protocol share.
cleared.result: MAX_LP_FEE is 1,000,000, which is below 2^20, so a valid fee never touches bit 22 (override flag 0x400000) or bit 23 (dynamic flag 0x800000) (src/libraries/LPFeeLibrary.sol:15-25). A pool is dynamic only when the fee field equals 0x800000 exactly (LPFeeLibrary.sol:30-32). isValidProtocolFee masks the low and the high 12 bits and compares them with 1001 and 1001 << 12 (src/libraries/ProtocolFeeLibrary.sol:25-32). I checked the function against the plain rule for one seventh of all 2^24 inputs. calculateSwapFee masks both inputs and returns p + l - floor(p * l / 1e6) (ProtocolFeeLibrary.sol:38-46). For every p from 0 to 1000 and a grid of l up to 1,000,000 the result stayed at or below 1,000,000 and was at least p and at least l, and it equalled p only when l was 0. The step fee is at least amountIn * swapFee / (1e6 - swapFee) rounded up, or the whole remainder on a partial step (src/libraries/SwapMath.sol:72-82, 104), so the protocol share floor((amountIn + feeAmount) * p / 1e6) cannot exceed it and the unchecked subtraction at src/libraries/Pool.sol:391-396 cannot wrap. The Slot0 setter masks the protocol fee to 24 bits before storing it (src/types/Slot0.sol:78-86).

cleared.check: Hook return data: which bits of the returned words the PoolManager uses, and whether dirty bits in a hook answer can change a value outside that hook's own pool.
cleared.result: parseSelector, parseFee and parseReturnDelta each load one full word at offsets 0x20, 0x60 and 0x40 of the returned bytes (src/libraries/ParseBytes.sol:9-28). The selector is compared as bytes4, so only the first four bytes of the first word count (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:152). The fee word is used only for a dynamic fee pool and only through an AND with 0x400000, an AND with 0xBFFFFF and a comparison with 1,000,000 (Hooks.sol:263, src/libraries/LPFeeLibrary.sol:61-78, src/libraries/Pool.sol:303-305), so bits above bit 23 are dropped whatever the compiler does with the assembly assignment, and a returned dynamic flag makes the fee fail validation. The delta word is split into two int128 halves and applied with checked arithmetic (Hooks.sol:266-279, 295-313). The hook is credited exactly what the caller is debited (src/PoolManager.sol:181-183, 224-226). Every value a hook can influence stays inside the pool that names that hook. The length rules are at least 32 bytes for every hook, exactly 64 bytes when a delta is parsed and exactly 96 bytes for beforeSwap (Hooks.sol:152, 166, 259).

cleared.check: Hook flag bits and the validity rule: do the 14 flags overlap, does operator precedence give the intended test, and which special addresses pass the rule.
cleared.result: The 14 flags are the single bits 13 down to 0 and ALL_HOOK_MASK is 2^14 - 1 (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:27-47). In Solidity the bitwise AND binds tighter than the comparison, so hasPermission tests (address & flag) != 0 and the last line of isValidHookAddress tests (address & mask) > 0 (Hooks.sol:126, 337-339). I enumerated all 16,384 low bit patterns. With a static fee exactly 5,183 are accepted, which is 3^4 * 2^6 - 1: each of the four return delta bits needs its action bit, and the all zero pattern is refused. The zero address is accepted only with a static fee, and an address without flags only with the dynamic fee value (Hooks.sol:124-126). The fixed cases in test/libraries/Hooks.t.sol:940-990 agree, including the refusal of an address whose only set bit is bit 14. Low addresses that pass include 0x10, 0x64, 0x100 and 0x101. A precompile or a codeless account at such an address cannot answer with 32 bytes that start with the hook selector, so the hooked action of that pool reverts (Hooks.sol:152-154). That is the recorded hook trust finding F-004 and needs victims to choose a pool with that hook address. The identity precompile at 0x04 echoes its input and would pass the selector test, and its address carries bit 2 without bit 6, which the rule refuses (Hooks.sol:112).

cleared.check: Tick bitmap word and bit positions, the compress function, and the unchecked int24 products in the search for the next initialized tick.
cleared.result: position returns the signed tick shifted right by 8 as the word index and the low 8 bits as the bit index (src/libraries/TickBitmap.sol:35-41). flipTick rejects a tick that is not a multiple of the spacing, divides, and builds the mapping slot from the 256 bit sign extended word index and the mapping slot, which is the encoding Solidity uses for an int16 index (TickBitmap.sol:47-75). For 200,000 random ticks and spacings the assembly compress equalled floor division, and the word index stayed inside int16 (-3466 to 3465 at spacing 1). The lte mask keeps bitPos + 1 low bits and the other mask clears the bits below bitPos (TickBitmap.sol:97, 110). The literal 1 in 1 << bitPos is evaluated as uint256. The largest magnitude the unchecked products can reach is 256 * 32767 = 8,388,352 for word index -1 at the maximum spacing, which is inside int24 (limit 8,388,608), and the swap loop then clamps the result to MIN_TICK and MAX_TICK (src/libraries/Pool.sol:351-356). MAX_TICK_SPACING is int16 max and initialize enforces the range 1 to 32767 (src/libraries/TickMath.sol:26-28, src/PoolManager.sol:119-120).

cleared.check: Tick info packing, LiquidityMath.addDelta and the liquidity cap per tick: can a width error let one account overflow gross, net or in range liquidity.
cleared.result: updateTick stores liquidityGross masked to 128 bits in the low half and liquidityNet shifted into the high half, which matches the declaration order of TickInfo (src/libraries/Pool.sol:68-77, 544-557). liquidityNet is computed with checked int128 arithmetic before the store (Pool.sol:543). addDelta masks x to 128 bits, sign extends y from 128 bits and reverts when any bit above bit 127 is set in the sum, which covers both overflow and underflow (src/libraries/LiquidityMath.sol:10-19). A transcription agreed with exact integer arithmetic on 200,000 random cases with dirty upper bits in x. tickSpacingToMaxLiquidityPerTick reproduces the four values in test/Tick.t.sol:115-141. For every spacing from 1 to 32767 the cap times the number of usable ticks is below 2^128 and the cap is below 2^127, so the sum of all tick liquidity fits uint128 and liquidityNet fits int128.

cleared.check: ERC-6909 id to currency conversion in mint and burn, and whether an id with high bits set can reach a balance or allowance of another id.
cleared.result: mint and burn truncate the id to 160 bits with fromId and use the truncated currency for the delta and toId of it for the claim balance, so an id with high bits set acts on the canonical id (src/PoolManager.sol:322-336, src/types/Currency.sol:110-118). The allowance and operator check in _burnFrom uses the same canonical id and the caller as spender (src/ERC6909Claims.sol:13-22). transfer, transferFrom and approve use the raw 256 bit id (src/ERC6909.sol:25-56). A balance at an id with high bits can never be minted, so those ids always hold zero and every transfer of them reverts in the checked subtraction. mint casts the amount with toInt128 before the negation, so the unchecked block at PoolManager.sol:323-328 cannot wrap (src/libraries/SafeCast.sol:56-59). The interface id 0x0f632fb3 equals the XOR of the seven ERC-6909 selectors.

cleared.check: Transient slot constants, the hash used for delta slots and the nonzero delta counter.
cleared.result: With a keccak implementation written for this unit and checked against the known digest of the empty string, keccak256 of ReservesOf, Currency, NonzeroDeltaCount and Unlocked minus one equal the four constants (src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:11-13, src/libraries/NonzeroDeltaCount.sol:9-10, src/libraries/Lock.sol:8). A delta slot is keccak256 of the 64 bytes (target, currency), both masked to 160 bits, in the same order in getDelta and applyDelta (src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:10-41). A delta slot equal to a fixed slot would need a preimage of a hash minus one. sync stores the currency masked to 160 bits together with the reserves, and resetCurrency clears only the currency (CurrencyReserves.sol:21-32). applyDelta adds with checked int256 arithmetic. _accountDelta returns early for a zero delta, decrements the counter only when a slot returns to zero and increments only when it leaves zero, so the wrapping subtraction in decrement is never reached at zero (src/PoolManager.sol:368-378, NonzeroDeltaCount.sol:28-34).

cleared.check: Position hash and pool id: byte layout of the assembly, dirty bits in the owner, and whether two different inputs can share a slot.
cleared.result: calculatePositionKey writes salt at offset 0x26, tickUpper at 0x06, tickLower at 0x03 and owner at 0 of free memory and hashes 58 bytes from offset 0x0c (src/libraries/Position.sol:54-66). I simulated the four overlapping writes on dirty memory for 2,000 random inputs with garbage above bit 160 of the owner. The result always equalled keccak256 of owner (20 bytes), tickLower (3), tickUpper (3) and salt (32), so the fields do not overlap and bits above the address fall outside the hashed range. The three words are zeroed afterwards. The owner is always msg.sender (src/PoolManager.sol:161). The pool id is keccak256 of the five words of the PoolKey in memory (src/types/PoolId.sol:11-15). The struct reaches memory through the ABI decoder of the external functions, which rejects dirty address, uint24 and int24 words, so one logical pool has one id.

cleared.check: Assembly memory use and cleanup: the ERC-20 transfer block, the hook call, the wrapped revert, the scratch space users and the storage readers.
cleared.result: The ERC-20 transfer writes 68 bytes at the free memory pointer without moving it, evaluates the call before the return data test, accepts empty return data or at least 32 bytes whose first word is 1, and zeroes the three words it used (src/types/Currency.sol:55-80). The output area is scratch word 0, and with empty return data the test does not read it. callHook allocates 32 bytes plus the return size rounded up to 32 after the call, which I checked for sizes 0 to 399, and copies the full return data (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:140-149). bubbleUpAndRevertWith lays out selector, address, selector word, the two offsets 0x80 and 0xa0 plus the padded size, the reason and a 4 byte context, and then reverts, so its use of memory past the pointer has no later reader (src/libraries/CustomRevert.sol:83-119). The delta slot hash and flipTick use only bytes 0 to 63 (src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:11-15, src/libraries/TickBitmap.sol:67-70). The revert helpers that take one argument write bytes 0 to 0x23, which is still scratch space (CustomRevert.sol:14-46). Extsload and Exttload return directly from assembly and write nothing but memory (src/Extsload.sol:10-63, src/Exttload.sol:10-39). No block writes below the free memory pointer outside the scratch space.

cleared.check: Every cast and every unchecked block in the non-test sources (30 occurrences of unchecked, 104 of assembly): can a wrap or a truncation give a caller a larger credit or a smaller debit.
cleared.result: take, mint and clear negate a value that toInt128 has limited to 0 through 2^127 - 1 (src/PoolManager.sol:292-296, 313-318, 323-328, src/libraries/SafeCast.sol:56-59). settle computes the payment with checked subtraction and casts it with toInt128 (PoolManager.sol:360-364). The unchecked protocol fee counter can only grow by amounts a swapper paid (src/ProtocolFees.sol:66-70). In Pool.swap the exact input remainder moves toward zero by at most its own size, the exact output remainder is reduced by at most itself, the protocol share is at most the step fee, the fee growth product stays below 2^255 because the whole swap amount must pass toInt128 at the end, and the final casts are function calls that revert inside the unchecked block (src/libraries/Pool.sol:371-407, 451-462). donate casts both amounts before negating (Pool.sol:469-479). The unchecked fee growth subtractions are modular by design and feed FullMath.mulDiv with a 128 bit liquidity and a divisor of 2^128, which cannot overflow (Pool.sol:497-510, 606-611, src/libraries/Position.sol:92-97). SafeCast compares the truncated value with the input for every narrowing cast (SafeCast.sol:16-59). The remaining unchecked blocks are in the math libraries that the two math units of cycle 1 and the two flow units of this cycle replayed. I found no cast or unchecked operation whose result an ordinary caller can push out of range without a revert.

cleared.check: Recount of every hex literal of six or more digits, the error selectors written as literals, and the TickMath and BitMath constants.
cleared.result: A script listed all such literals in the non-test sources. Each address mask has 40 digits of f, each 128 bit mask 32, each 24 bit mask 6, and the two selector masks keep the top four bytes. The literals 0xa9059cbb, 0x93dafdf1, 0xd4d8f3e6, 0xf5c787f1, 0x4323a555, 0x4f2461b8 and 0x00bfc921 equal the first four hash bytes of transfer(address,uint256), SafeCastOverflow(), TickMisaligned(int24,int24), PriceOverflow(), NotEnoughLiquidity(), InvalidPriceOrLiquidity() and InvalidPrice(). Each of the 20 TickMath multipliers read from the file is within 0.5 of 2^128 divided by sqrt(1.0001)^(2^i). With those constants getSqrtPriceAtTick is strictly increasing over all 1,774,545 ticks, returns MIN_SQRT_PRICE and MAX_SQRT_PRICE at the ends, and getTickAtSqrtPrice inverts it at every tick and one unit below. The two BitMath functions returned the exact bit index for every single bit value, every low and high mask and 200,000 random values. This repeats the cycle 1 result with a separate transcription.

cleared.check: Do the 21 networks execute the bit level instructions of this unit as the code expects, and what do codeless and precompile targets return to a transfer shaped call.
cleared.result: I sent one 980 byte creation payload with eth_call and no to address to the RPC endpoint of each network in state/networks.json on 2026-11-22. It returns 28 words: SIGNEXTEND 15 and 2 on values with dirty upper bits, SAR 128, the BalanceDelta pack of (-5, -7), a Slot0 tick read, the delta slot hash, TLOAD before and after TSTORE, SDIV and SMOD of MIN_TICK by 60, a BYTE table lookup, SHL, SHR by 256, MULMOD by 2^256 - 1 and a 160 bit AND. It also makes four calls with the 68 byte calldata of transfer(address,uint256) and a 32 byte output area at memory 0. All 21 networks returned the 28 expected words. A codeless address and the ecrecover precompile at 0x01 return success with empty return data and leave memory word 0 unchanged. The identity precompile at 0x04 returns the 68 input bytes, whose first word is not 1, and sha256 at 0x02 returns a 32 byte hash. Under src/types/Currency.sol:64-74 a take in currency 0x01 or in a codeless currency therefore counts as paid and moves nothing, which only debits the caller (src/PoolManager.sol:294-295), and a take in currency 0x02 or 0x04 reverts. sync decodes a 32 byte result, so it reverts on empty data and reads a constant on 0x02 and 0x04, and the difference between sync and settle is then zero (Currency.sol:94, PoolManager.sol:358-360). No positive delta arises without a real balance increase on any of the 21 networks through these targets.
cleared.source: eth_call on the 21 rpc URLs in research/network-risk/state/networks.json; src/types/Currency.sol:55-80, 90-96; src/PoolManager.sol:279-297, 349-364

In the inheritance order of PoolManager the slots are owner 0, protocolFeesAccrued 1, protocolFeeController 2, isOperator 3, balanceOf 4, allowance 5 and _pools 6 (src/ProtocolFees.sol:15-24, src/ERC6909.sol:15-19, src/PoolManager.sol:80-93). cleared.check: Compiler bugs listed for solc 0.8.26: does the source text contain the patterns that the Solidity bug list names, in particular the Yul optimizer bug SOL-2026-7 of 22 October 2026.
cleared.result: bugs_by_version.json lists eight entries for 0.8.26. Seven need constructs the non-test sources do not contain: a recursive storage struct with a dynamic array (two entries), a custom error with named arguments inside require (the four require calls at src/libraries/FullMath.sol:30, 113 and src/libraries/BitMath.sol:13, 32 have no error argument), delete on a bytes element under the legacy pipeline, mutual recursion (two entries), and a storage array at the end of storage. SOL-2026-7 needs a variable that is used to compute memory or storage addresses, is reassigned in a loop or branch, and yields two addresses with different constant offsets that coincide at run time, followed by a load or an equal store. In the handwritten assembly the only reassigned address variables are memptr, startSlot and calldataptr in the loops of src/Extsload.sol:18-63 and src/Exttload.sol:18-39. Those functions never read back what they stored and never store a value twice, so neither affected optimizer step has anything to replace. Every other block derives its addresses from constants or from a pointer assigned once (src/types/Currency.sol:57, src/libraries/Position.sol:55, src/libraries/Hooks.sol:142, src/libraries/TickBitmap.sol:67-73, src/libraries/Pool.sol:547). Storage and memory structs are reached through hashed mapping slots or pointers that are assigned once, and the swap loop changes no address variable by a constant (Pool.sol:344-437). The Solidity team states that the condition cannot be decided from Solidity source because it depends on the intermediate Yul code. I did not compile anything, so the compiler generated code remains unchecked and lead L-028 stays open.

cleared.check: Which invariants of flash accounting and custody does the code enforce, and where. This is the list that the other items of this unit try to break.
cleared.result: I1, lock. Every function that writes a delta carries onlyWhenUnlocked (src/PoolManager.sol:96-99 and the modifiers at 147, 189, 258, 291, 300, 305, 310, 322, 332). The flag is set only at line 107, cleared only at line 113, and unlock reverts when it is already set (105). I2, closure. unlock returns only when NonzeroDeltaCount is zero (112). _accountDelta raises the counter when a slot leaves zero and lowers it when a slot returns to zero (368-378), so the counter equals the number of nonzero (account, currency) slots. I3, credits. A positive delta comes from four places only: settle, which adds msg.value when no ERC-20 is synced or the checked rise of balanceOf since sync (349-364); burn, which lowers an ERC-6909 balance by the same amount (332-336, src/ERC6909.sol:85-89); a pool action whose amounts Pool computes (159-183, 206-226, 268-270); and a hook delta that is subtracted from the caller in the same step (src/libraries/Hooks.sol:230, 242, 312). I4, debits. take and mint debit the nominal amount before any external call (294, 326). clear can only bring a positive delta to zero (310-319). I5, custody. The PoolManager sends assets only through Currency.transfer in take (295) and in collectProtocolFees (src/ProtocolFees.sol:56), each after an equal bookkeeping decrease (294 and ProtocolFees.sol:55). I6, one payment bracket. There is one synced currency slot. sync overwrites it (286) or resets it for the native asset (283), an ERC-20 settle resets it (361), and settle rejects msg.value while it is set (356). I7, claims. ERC-6909 balances change only in transfer, transferFrom, _mint and _burn with checked arithmetic (src/ERC6909.sol:25-48, 79-89). From I1 to I7 it follows that for every currency id the PoolManager balance stays at or above pool reserves plus claims plus accrued protocol fees, as long as four properties of the chain and the token hold: T1, balanceOf(PoolManager) of a currency changes only by transfers to or from the PoolManager and by the transferred amount; T2, no second currency id draws on the same balance in another unit; T3, msg.value arrives in full; T4, transient storage is one store per transaction that follows call and revert semantics. The code checks none of T1 to T4.

cleared.check: Exhaustive search for a sequence of unlock, sync, settle, settleFor, take, clear, mint, burn, ERC-6909 transfer and direct payment by one account that leaves the account richer or the PoolManager short, in seven currency settings.
cleared.result: I wrote a state model of the settlement layer from the source lines and explored every reachable state, with claims per id capped at 2 and each delta capped at plus or minus 4, amounts 0, 1 and 2, and the whole sequence treated as one transaction so that a sync survives between unlocks. The search asserts in every state that the counter equals the number of nonzero delta slots and never goes below zero. Settings and results: native plus ERC-20, 35,859 states, no gain; native plus an ERC-20 face that mirrors the native balance one to one and can transfer (CELO token shape), with native sends that reach the PoolManager without a call, 31,628 states, no gain; the same face without a working transfer (Polygon 0x1010 and LegacyERC20ETH shape), 9,709 states, no gain; a face that reports floor(native / 3) and moves 3 base units per unit, without forced native sends, 48,488 states, no gain; a wrapper that credits the sender of native value (WETH9 shape), 214,118 states, no gain; a deposit ledger that credits the sender and has no transfer (EntryPoint shape), 10,872 states, no gain. In none of these did the PoolManager end below its obligations. The one setting with a gain is the scaled face together with forced native sends, which is recorded in the Arc item below.

cleared.check: Re-entry into someone else's unlock: a recipient of a native payout, a token with callbacks or a hook gets control while a victim is between its pool action, sync, payment and settle. Can it take the victim's payment, make the victim pay twice, or leave the victim without what it paid for.
cleared.result: The victim script is unlock, an action that leaves it owing 1 unit and holding a claim, sync of the currency, payment, settle, return. The attacker may run up to two operations of its own in each of the six gaps, which is more than any real callback allows. Five settings were searched to the end: ERC-20 payment (2,235,193 states, 157 completed runs), native payment (1,211,637 and 130), payment through a one to one native face (1,696,802 and 48), native payment on a chain that has such a face (943,455 and 50), payment through a scaled face (3,811,569 and 393). In every completed run the attacker's wallet did not grow, the victim paid exactly its amount and kept its claim. Runs in which the attacker booked the victim's payment with settleFor, re-synced, or reset the sync with sync(address(0)) all end with a nonzero slot and revert at src/PoolManager.sol:112. A callee can therefore make the surrounding unlock revert, which it could also do by reverting itself, and cannot change who is credited in a transaction that succeeds.

cleared.check: A stale sync: sync needs no lock, and its two slots are the only settlement state that can outlive an unlock. What can a party gain from a sync left behind inside one transaction, and what would follow if a network failed to wipe transient storage between transactions.
cleared.result: unlock ends with the flag false and the counter zero or it reverts (src/PoolManager.sol:105-113), so after any successful call the lock flag and all deltas are zero and only the synced currency and reserves can remain (src/PoolManager.sol:279-288, src/libraries/CurrencyReserves.sol:21-32). The model treats a whole sequence as one transaction and found no gain from a sync that survives between unlocks. The effects that remain are these. A later settle with msg.value reverts with NonzeroNativeValue until someone calls sync again (src/PoolManager.sol:356). collectProtocolFees for that ERC-20 reverts (src/ProtocolFees.sol:49-52). The next settle without a new sync credits the caller with every rise of that balance since the stale sync, which inside one transaction can only be the caller's own payment or an inflow it triggered. If a network kept transient storage across transactions, the same reading gives two consequences and no more: native payers who do not call sync first would revert until the slot is reset, and a party could leave a sync in one transaction and book unsolicited inflows, such as a positive rebase, in a later one. Deposits of other users are not exposed, because every ERC-20 settle resets the slot and every payer that follows the interface comment calls sync first (src/interfaces/IPoolManager.sol:165-171). A leak of the lock flag or of a delta across transactions would be a different and total failure, and the code gives no path to it under call and revert semantics.

cleared.check: Protocol fee collection at a moment chosen by an outsider, on networks where the controller is an adapter with a public collect function: before a sync, between sync and settle, inside an unlock, and on networks where the native asset has an ERC-20 face.
cleared.result: I added a third party fee withdrawal of one unit, allowed at any point except for the ERC-20 that is currently synced, to the model and searched the native plus ERC-20 setting (75,072 states), the one to one face setting (67,659) and the scaled face setting (100,064). No sequence gave the attacker a gain or left the PoolManager below its remaining obligations. The reading agrees: collectProtocolFees lowers protocolFeesAccrued with a checked subtraction before it transfers (src/ProtocolFees.sol:54-56), writes no delta and no transient slot, and reverts for the synced ERC-20 in both lock states (src/ProtocolFees.sol:49-52), so it can neither raise a settle credit nor pay out more than was accrued. _isUnlocked is declared and never called (src/ProtocolFees.sol:60, src/PoolManager.sol:392-394). On a network with a native face, a withdrawal of native fees while the face is synced lowers the face balance, and the settle that follows credits less or reverts in the checked subtraction (src/PoolManager.sol:360). That can only happen inside the transaction of the party that holds the bracket.

cleared.check: Arc: USDC is the native asset with 18 decimals and also answers at 0x3600000000000000000000000000000000000000 with 6 decimals. The face rounds down, so a settle bracket on the face can credit one face unit for less than 10^12 base units. How much can an ordinary account take that way.
cleared.result: In the model, a face that reports floor(native / S) gives a gain only when native value can reach the PoolManager without a call while the face is synced. Each round is sync(face), a forced send of the missing base units, settle, and a native take that restores the remainder, and it turns a native debt of 1 base unit into a credit of 1 face unit, a gain of at most S - 1 base units. With S = 3 the search found a sequence of 7 rounds inside one unlock that took all 13 base units of the toy PoolManager, so the mechanism is real and repeatable. Without forced sends the gain is zero, because settle rejects msg.value while the face is synced (src/PoolManager.sol:356), the PoolManager has no receive or fallback function, and the face moves whole units only. On Arc S is 10^12 base units, which is 0.000001 USDC. At block 32,594,756 the PoolManager held 2,444,955,282,313,718,484,324,471 base units and the face reported 2,444,955,282,313, which is the floor of that figure divided by 10^12. The base fee was 20 gwei in each of 21 consecutive blocks ending at 32,597,012 and eth_gasPrice returned 25 gwei. A call that carries value costs at least 9,000 gas, which is 1.8 * 10^14 base units at 20 gwei, about 180 times the largest possible gain of one round, before the cost of sync, settle, take and the forced send. An account that pays the base fee loses money on every round. I did not test whether a forced send by SELFDESTRUCT is accepted on Arc; the stablecoin unit reports that it is. This agrees with the earlier clearance by that unit and adds the per round bound and the fee figures.

cleared.result: I computed the selectors of all 33 external functions of the PoolManager and of the 13 calls it issues with a keccak implementation checked against known digests. None of the 13 outgoing selectors (a9059cbb, 70a08231, 91dd7346, dc98354e, 6fe7e6eb, 259982e5, 9f063efc, 21d0ee70, 6c2bbe7e, 575e24b4, b47b2fb1, b6a8b0fa, e1b4af69) equals a selector of the PoolManager. cleared.check: Width and sign at the settlement entry points: amounts of 2^127 or more, accumulation of many deltas in one slot, an id with high bits in mint and burn, and the three unchecked blocks in PoolManager.sol.
cleared.result: take, mint, burn, clear and settle convert the amount with SafeCast.toInt128, which reverts for 2^127 or more (src/libraries/SafeCast.sol:56-59; src/PoolManager.sol:294, 313, 326, 334, 364). The unchecked blocks at lines 292, 316 and 323 cover only the negation of a value that is at most 2^127 - 1 and calls to functions whose own arithmetic stays checked, since a called function does not inherit the block. A delta slot holds an int256 and is updated with a checked addition (src/libraries/CurrencyDelta.sol:37), and each update is below 2^127 in size, so a slot cannot wrap. mint and burn truncate the id to 160 bits and use the truncated value for both the delta and the claim (src/PoolManager.sol:324-327, 333-335; src/types/Currency.sol:110-118). clear compares the int128 amount with the int256 slot, so it succeeds only for an exact positive match or for zero against zero (310-319), which is what test/PoolManager.clear.t.sol expects in its seven cases.

Sync.t.sol: sync outside an unlock sets the synced currency (36-41, source 279-288); a settle after sync with no payment applies no delta (161-200, source 358-364); a settle without sync credits msg.value, here zero, and the tokens sent stay in the PoolManager (207-253, source 353-354); settle with value after a token sync reverts with NonzeroNativeValue (255-275 and PoolManager.t.sol:976-989, source 356); sync(address(0)) after a token sync allows a native settle (300-339, source 281-283); a second settle credits nothing (341 onward, source 361). cleared.check: Arc: the CallFrom precompile at 0x1800000000000000000000000000000000000003 starts a call on behalf of Memo and Multicall3From. Does that inner call run with transient storage of its own, which would separate PoolManager deltas from payouts inside one unlock, and can a contract in the middle of a transaction use it to act as another account at the PoolManager.
cleared.result: No to both, in the main branch of the client. The precompile builds an ordinary CALL input with the chosen sender as caller and zero value (call_from.rs, decode_child_call). ArcEvm::init_subcall rejects static context and value, rejects a substituted sender that is neither the calling helper nor the transaction signer, and then pushes the child through the same frame stack and the same journal as every other call, with a journal checkpoint taken from that journal (evm.rs, init_subcall and complete_subcall). A child frame on the same journal sees and writes the same transient storage as its parent, so the lock flag, the deltas and the counter of the PoolManager stay one consistent store (src/PoolManager.sol:104-114, src/libraries/NonzeroDeltaCount.sol:12-34). Memo passes msg.sender as the sender (Memo.sol, memo), which closes the part the stablecoin unit left unread. A contract that is not the signer therefore cannot reach the PoolManager as someone else, and the ERC-6909 functions that trust msg.sender (src/ERC6909.sol:25-64) keep their meaning. I read the main branch and did not confirm which release mainnet runs, and I did not read revm itself for where transient storage lives; the stablecoin unit did.

cleared.check: Tempo: from hardfork T5 three precompiles on the Implicit Approval List (FeeManager, StablecoinDEX, TIP20ChannelReserve) may move TIP-20 tokens out of any account without an allowance through system_transfer_from. Can an ordinary account make one of them pull tokens out of the PoolManager, which would lower a balance without a take.
cleared.result: No path found in the client source at commit 697ea97. system_transfer_from is not part of the token ABI and accepts only a listed precompile as caller (tip20/mod.rs:939-980). Every call site passes the direct caller of the precompile as the account to pull from: the DEX in transfer_from and decrement_balance_or_transfer_from, which its dispatcher feeds with msg_sender for place, placeFlip, withdraw, cancel and both swaps (stablecoin_dex/mod.rs:299-352, stablecoin_dex/dispatch.rs:17-66); the fee AMM in two places with msg_sender (tip_fee_manager/amm.rs:239 and 360); the channel reserve in two places with msg_sender (tip20_channel_reserve/mod.rs:215 and 380). The PoolManager would have to be the direct caller, and it can send only transfer(address,uint256), balanceOf(address), unlockCallback, the IHooks selectors and empty calldata (src/types/Currency.sol:48-73, 94; src/PoolManager.sol:110; src/libraries/Hooks.sol:131-137), which the stablecoin unit found these precompiles reject. Fee collection before a transaction pulls from the fee payer, which is the signer or a sponsor that signed. Custody rule I5 of this unit therefore holds on Tempo apart from issuer roles, which are recorded elsewhere. The source comment says that pulling only from msg.sender is a guideline enforced at each call site and not inside system_transfer_from, so a precompile added to the list later needs the same reading.

If the caller synced the wrapper first, settle credits that amount of wrapped currency to the caller (src/PoolManager.sol:358-360) and the native debit of the same amount from take remains (src/PoolManager.sol:294). The caller must pay it with msg.value before unlock returns (src/PoolManager.sol:112). Without a prior sync the wrapped tokens stay in the PoolManager as an unaccounted surplus and the caller still owes the native amount. cleared.check: Whether Jenner gives BNB an ERC-20 face through CAS20 or another reserved address (critic lead from cycle 1).
cleared.result: Not in the client source. The CAS20 token dispatcher keeps balances in the token's own storage and has no entry that reads or moves an account's BNB balance. Every CAS20 entry point reverts when value is attached. The factory, policy registry and activation registry are the only other routed addresses. The millisecond timestamp precompile at 0x70 was found in the precompile table only. Its source file was not located, so its answers to transfer and balanceOf calldata are open. cleared.check: Whether the storage slot alias of the C-Chain (bit 248 cleared) lets anyone make two slots of the PoolManager collide.
cleared.result: No. The fixed slots 0 to 6 have a zero first byte. All other slots are keccak256 outputs or such an output plus an offset below 7 (src/libraries/StateLibrary.sol:324-326, src/libraries/Pool.sol:83-91, src/libraries/TickBitmap.sol:66-73, src/ERC6909.sol:15-19). A collision needs two hashes that agree in 255 bits. extsload exposes the alias for reads only (src/Extsload.sol:10-15). The transient slots are not rewritten. Hooks and tokens with hand-picked slots are covered by the finding of this cycle.

cleared.check: Where the Continuous Execution engine discards transient storage between two transactions of one block, and whether end of block operations run contract code (critic lead and unit lead from cycle 1).
cleared.result: saexec.Execute opens a new state database for each block and applies each transaction with core.ApplyTransaction. libevm's TransitionDb calls StateDB.Prepare for every message (core/state_transition.go line 436) and Prepare assigns a new transient storage map (core/state/statedb.go line 1335). End of block operations are balance and nonce writes (hook.Op.ApplyTo). FinishExecutingBlock moves non-AVAX asset balances. Neither makes an EVM call. A stale sync therefore cannot survive into another transaction. The public endpoint has no eth_simulateV1, so this rests on the source at tag v1.15.3 and the pinned libevm commit.

cleared.check: Whether any execution path on the C-Chain gives msg.sender the zero address, which is the stored protocolFeeController there (src/ProtocolFees.sol:36, src/ProtocolFees.sol:48).
cleared.result: None in the engine source. The only call that is not a signed transaction is the EIP-4788 system call, whose caller is 0xffff...fffe and whose target has no code on the C-Chain. Cross-chain transactions never run contract code. A signed transaction needs a signature that recovers to its sender. This replaces the documentation-only basis of the cycle 1 item.

cleared.check: Whether a cross-chain export can debit the PoolManager, and whether an import that credits it gives anyone a delta.
cleared.result: An export input must carry a signature whose recovered address equals the debited address (verifyCredentials), which no one can produce for a contract. An import adds AVAX to the named address with AddBalance and runs no code, so the PoolManager balance rises and nobody is credited, because native credit is msg.value only (src/PoolManager.sol:353-354).

cleared.check: Whether the protocol-level balance credits of Bor (base fee to the burn contract, tip to the coinbase) can reach the PoolManager balance between sync(0x1010) and settle.
cleared.result: No. Both credits go to addresses fixed in the chain config (params/config.go, BurntContract and Coinbase maps) and are applied after the transaction's execution ends (core/state_transition.go lines 634 to 644). The PoolManager is neither address.

cleared.check: Whether transient storage of one user transaction is visible to the next under the client source read this cycle.
cleared.result: No. Bor calls StateDB.Prepare at core/state_transition.go line 550 and resets the map at core/state/statedb.go line 3051. BSC calls it at core/state_transition.go line 623 and resets at core/state/statedb.go line 1532. Bor state sync records get the same reset through PrepareStateSyncContext since Austin, and Parlia system messages through applyMessage. This agrees with the two transaction simulation the critic ran on both endpoints in cycle 1.

cleared.check: Opcode differential for the call patterns of the PoolManager: CALL with and without value, the copy of return data into memory, calls to addresses without code, TLOAD and TSTORE, in the three clients.
cleared.result: The bodies of opCall, EVM.Call, opTload and opTstore in Bor v2.11.0, BSC master and libevm d398bc4dbe41 follow the go-ethereum pattern. A call to an address without code that is no precompile returns success with empty data, and return data shorter than the output area leaves the rest of the area untouched, which is what the success test at src/types/Currency.sol:64-74 expects. BSC adds a branch that skips the value transfer when the caller is the system address and a prefix route to CAS20 native code after Jenner. Avalanche adds the precompile override hook and the storage slot rewrite. MCOPY, PUSH0, SELFBALANCE and gas forwarding were not re-read in source and rest on the cycle 1 probes.

cleared.check: Known weakness: the validator counting flaw in the light client precompile 0x67 fixed by BEP-682 in Pasteur, and the staking and governance fixes of BEP-695.
cleared.result: They concern the BNB Chain bridge and validator administration. The PoolManager never calls 0x67, and a call from it with any tested calldata reverts. A forged bridge message would affect bridged BNB supply and token issuers, which is outside what an ordinary account can turn against pool funds directly.

cleared.check: Known weaknesses disclosed for Bor in 2026: the Austin fixes (unbounded state sync gas, unbounded TxDependency field) and the Uburu and v2.11.x security releases.
cleared.result: The disclosed Austin issues are denial of service paths in block processing that a block producer or a sender of many bridge events could use. They delay all transactions and do not change PoolManager state. The v2.11.0 and v2.11.1 notes list state sync fetching, span lookup, witness and header checks. None changes how a transaction executes against a contract. The notes give no detail on what Uburu changed inside the StateReceiver, which stays an open lead from cycle 1.

cleared.check: Known weaknesses around Helicon: the gas floor of ACP-194 and the worst-case balance bounds.
cleared.result: The floor charges a sender at least half of the gas limit and closes a queue flooding path. The bounds decide whether a transaction may be included. Both act on the fee payer of a transaction. The PoolManager never pays gas, and a revert inside a transaction still rolls back all PoolManager state, transient storage included.

cleared.check: Sweep of all 18 precompiles with the PoolManager as sender: empty calldata with zero value and with 1 ETH (P1), transfer(address,uint256) with zero and 1e18 (P2), balanceOf(PoolManager) (P3) and all ten IHooks selectors with well-formed arguments (P5). Follow-up on each target that did not revert.
cleared.result: No precompile yields a credit or an unpaid outflow. ECRECOVER and P256VERIFY return empty data: take succeeds and moves nothing while the caller is debited, and sync reverts because the Solidity decoder needs 32 bytes, so no credit can arise. SHA256, RIPEMD160 and IDENTITY return 32 bytes or more that depend only on the input, so the value read at sync equals the value read at settle and paid is zero; their answer to transfer is a digest or the echoed calldata, never the word 1, so take reverts. The other precompiles fail on the input lengths the PoolManager can produce. ETH sent to a precompile address with a native take stays there and the caller owes it. The sync results on the existing mainnet deployment (reverts for 0x01, 0x100 and an empty address, succeeds for 0x02, 0x03, 0x04) agree with this reading of the source; I used them as a behavioural reference and did not compare code.

cleared.check: Same 15 call shapes against the beacon roots, history storage, deposit, withdrawal request and consolidation request contracts, and whether the PoolManager can be made to file a withdrawal or consolidation request.
cleared.result: Three contracts revert on every shape. The two request contracts answer only the empty call without value, with the fee. A request needs a call of exactly 56 or 96 bytes that carries the fee. The PoolManager sends to a caller-chosen address only empty calldata (native take), 36 bytes by STATICCALL (sync), 68 bytes without value (token take) or at least 228 bytes without value (hook calls), so it cannot file a request. A request with the PoolManager as source would in any case only act on a validator whose withdrawal credentials already point at the PoolManager.

cleared.check: Whether any special address on mainnet can serve as a hook that the PoolManager accepts, so that a hook call has a lasting side effect made with the PoolManager as sender.
cleared.result: A hook call is kept only if the return data is at least 32 bytes and starts with the called selector. Of all swept targets only the identity precompile does that, and 0x04 fails the address check because it sets the after-swap returns-delta bit without the after-swap bit. An EIP-7702 delegation to a precompile runs empty code, so it cannot proxy the identity precompile. The valid special addresses (0x10, 0x100, beacon roots, deposit contract, WETH9, system address, the PoolManager itself) return empty data or revert, which makes the PoolManager revert. A pool whose hook is 0x100 or any empty address with bit 8 or 9 set accepts deposits and reverts every removal; that is the hook finding of cycle 1 with actor pool-creator and needs no new entry.

cleared.check: Native payout (P1) to contracts that book incoming ETH to the sender: WETH9, Lido stETH, frxETHMinter, EntryPoint v0.6, v0.7 and v0.8, the OptimismPortal of OP Mainnet and Base, and the TokenJar. The call was made by the PoolManager address with an unrelated transaction origin. Does the caller end up owing less than what left, with or without a sync and settle around the payout?
cleared.result: take debits the caller the full amount of currency address(0) before the transfer. With sync(WETH9) before and settle after, the caller is credited exactly the 1e18 WETH that the PoolManager received for 1 ETH, so the PoolManager converts 1:1 and both legs are booked. For stETH the credit is 1 wei less than the debit. EntryPoint credits its deposit ledger, which sync can read, but EntryPoint has no transfer function, so that credit can only become an ERC-6909 claim nobody can redeem. A portal deposit is sent from the aliased PoolManager address to the PoolManager's own address on the L2, where no one can sign for either. The OP Mainnet L1StandardBridge refuses a contract caller. In every case the value is booked to the PoolManager and the caller owes the full native amount. Without the sync bracket the received tokens are an unbooked surplus. This is a loss for a caller who names such a recipient and gives an attacker nothing. The op-stack units recorded the same behaviour for L2 predeploys.

cleared.check: Whether a zero amount call made by the PoolManager, either take(address(0), X, 0) with empty calldata or take(X, to, 0) as X.transfer(to, 0), changes a balance the PoolManager holds on the targets swept.
cleared.result: Nothing is owed for a zero amount, so these calls are free pokes with the PoolManager as sender. On the swept targets they do nothing: WETH9 deposits zero, Lido reverts on a zero value submit, the EntryPoint ledger is unchanged, stETH.transfer(to, 0) from the PoolManager leaves its balance unchanged in simulation, and precompiles and system contracts return data or revert. The PoolManager has no fallback or receive function and none of its own functions matches the transfer(address,uint256) selector or an IHooks selector, so it cannot be made to call itself successfully. A token that pays or rebases its holder on such a poke would fall under the finding in this file.

cleared.check: Faces on mainnet: can one balance be reached under two currency ids so that a payment is credited twice or one id drains the other. Checked ETH against WETH9, tokens with two entry points (the PoolManager holds 258.6 TUSD and 4,089 SNX), and a ledger credited by a value transfer (EntryPoint).
cleared.result: ETH and WETH9 are separate balances. There is one sync slot, each sync overwrites both transient values, and a credit is the measured rise since the latest sync, so one transfer in is credited once under one id. Each take sends at most what it debits under the id named. Over all ids that share a balance, credits minus debits equal the real change. A native payment cannot be counted under an ERC-20 id because settle rejects msg.value while an ERC-20 is synced, settle and settleFor are the only payable functions, and sync(address(0)) followed by a later sync re-reads the balance. I did not call the second entry point of TUSD or SNX on chain.

cleared.check: Opcode and call semantics the PoolManager relies on, read in the Osaka execution specification: transient storage lifetime and rollback, value transfer order, static context, return data after failed calls, gas forwarding and precompile dispatch.
cleared.result: Transient storage is created per transaction and rolled back with the frame, value moves before callee code runs and is undone on failure, a failed or underfunded call returns 0 with empty return data, and the callee receives at most 63/64 of the gas. The source handles each case by reverting: a failed native or token transfer reverts with a wrapped error, a failed hook call reverts, and a failed balanceOf reverts through the decoder. No path continues after a failed external call, so the gas rule can make an operation fail and cannot make it half succeed.

cleared.check: Known weaknesses of mainnet execution clients, precompiles and system contracts from the last two years: could an ordinary account use any of them against funds in the PoolManager.
cleared.result: The incidents I found are liveness and consensus faults: the Reth state root stall of 2025-09-02, Nethermind nodes rejecting a canonical block at the Fusaka fork, and client fixes for MODEXP in Geth and P256VERIFY in Besu that the Fusaka retrospective lists. A node that stalls or rejects a block does not execute a different result for an included transaction, and settlement in core is atomic inside one transaction. The PoolManager calls a precompile only when a caller names one as currency, hook or recipient, and the sweep shows those calls give the caller nothing. I did not search vendor advisory databases one by one, and I did not find a published mainnet bug in TSTORE, TLOAD or CALL handling.

cleared.check: Whether the public reward and rebase triggers that exist today for tokens the PoolManager holds move value that a caller could book: Compound v2 claimComp, Compound v3 CometRewards.claim, Olympus staking rebase, OUSD and OETH vault rebase, Aave aToken growth.
cleared.result: At block 26471590 claimComp(PoolManager) paid 0 COMP, the Comet claim reverted, the Olympus rebase changed nothing, and the Origin vault calls are restricted. aToken balances grow with time and with flash loan premiums; a caller who pays a premium to move the index receives only the PoolManager's small share of it back, which is less than the premium. No value can be taken through these today. The mechanism stays open for tokens with a paying trigger and is recorded as the finding.
